The paper appears to report data that the authors collected from people or animals, but we found no ethics statement. Such data need one: approval by an ethics committee, or a reason why none was needed. We based this on the sentences below. Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). install.packages() calls were found in 1 code file.

File name install.packages() calls found
forPaperTierComparison.R install.packages(“abtest”)

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In 3 code files, libraries/imports were at multiple places (i.e., with more than 3 non-comment lines in between).

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 34 distinct packages/libraries: abtest, argparse, coda, collections, datetime, dplyr, fitz, ggplot2, glob, grid, irr, jaspGraphs, json, kableExtra, knitr, loo, MCMCpack, os, pandas, parallel, patchwork, pathlib, pdfplumber, Polychrome, random, re, remotes, rlang, rstan, scales, stringr, tidyr, tools, utils. Reproducible Environment

The repository pins its analysis environment via a sessionInfo() record. Declared R version: 4.5.2. The sessionInfo() record lists 94 package versions.

No list of the Python packages the code needs (a requirements.txt, environment.yml, Pipfile.lock, poetry.lock, uv.lock or pyproject.toml) was found anywhere in the repository. Without one, the package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and they may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing a requirements.txt that lists each package with its version (for example the output of pip freeze).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 312 columns across 29 data files.

Issues Identified

62 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 29 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

We ran the paper’s 13 R scripts and 8 Python scripts in the order they depend on each other, each in an isolated container, for at most 5 minutes per script. Metacheck detected version information that can be used to install specific versions of software for the reproducibility run. We recommend retrying the reproducibility check with recorded_versions = TRUE. This will install the required R packages, if still available. As this takes a long time, this setting is not implemented on this shared server. 2 identical copies of these scripts, which other links in the paper lead to, were not run again.

10 of 21 scripts ran to the end: 5 did not reproduce, 3 could not run because a package or program was not available, and 3 did not finish within our time limit.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

Files are missing from your deposit.

  • countMergedExclusions.py reads jesp_articles_cleaned.csv.
  • prepareDataForReview.py reads combined_journals_withlinks.csv.

The script stops at the line that reads the file.

  1. Find the file on your computer.
  2. Add it to the deposit, in the folder where the script looks for it.
  3. If you cannot share it, for example for privacy reasons, say so in the README, and explain where readers can get it and where to put it.

A file may have been renamed.

  • cleanData.py reads xge_articles.csv; your deposit holds xge_articles_cleaned.csv.

Check whether they are the same file. If so, use one name in both the script and the deposit.

A package could not be installed.

  • forPaperOther.R needs jaspGraphs.
  • forPaperPrimaryFigures.R needs jaspGraphs.
  • forPaperTierComparison.R needs jaspGraphs.

jaspGraphs could not be installed in our run. Record the versions you used (in R, renv::init() writes them to a renv.lock file) and your R version, and say in the README where any package that is not on CRAN comes from.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • forPaperBayes.R
  • forPaperOpenData.R
  • forPaperPreregistration.R

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Metacheck can’t automatically establish what caused the error, or how it should be improved.

  • countExcludedArticles.py
  • mergeJournals.py

The error message of each script is in the table above.

Other problems in the files

  • prepareDataForReview.py calls os.chdir(), which sets the folder the script runs in. We replaced the call with one that does nothing, so the script ran from the top folder of the project. A folder on your own computer does not exist on another; paths written from the project’s top folder work everywhere.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 34 statistical tests reported in the paper, 0 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 14 R code files.

Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), source() calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

File paths

Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 14 scripts: 7 ran without error, 0 errored, 3 timed out, 3 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

Dependency-unavailable errors

3 scripts could not run because their own dependency is unavailable — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper’s code, so it does not force the traffic light red.

Other changes we made to run the code

Stan files in the syntax Stan removed in version 2.33 were given the newer syntax, and Git LFS pointers (placeholders a GitHub archive holds instead of the file) were replaced by the deposit’s copy of the file. Updating the Stan files, and depositing the files themselves, solves this.

File Change
Data_analysis/LogGC.stan Stan from before 2.33: array declarations
Data_analysis/stateSpace.stan Stan from before 2.33: array declarations
Data_analysis/stateSpaceOldSsm.stan Stan from before 2.33: array declarations
Preregistration/Analysis code/5PL.stan Stan from before 2.33: array declarations
Preregistration/Analysis code/stateSpace.stan Stan from before 2.33: array declarations

Calls that install packages in the code

5 calls to install.packages(), groundhog, checkpoint, renv, pacman and the like were replaced, since they install packages themselves: groundhog.library() and p_load() by library(), the others by a statement that does nothing. The scripts ran with the packages installed before the run.

Run by another script

1 script is run by another script with source(), so it was not run on its own: each script runs in a fresh R process, and on its own a sourced script lacks the packages and objects the sourcing script sets up first. Its outcome is part of the sourcing script’s outcome.

>   inYear <- if (is.na(tests$year[i])) rep(TRUE, nrow(d)) else d$Year == tests$year[i]
>   top <- inYear & d$tier == "TopTier"
>   mid <- inYear & d$tier == "MidTier"
>   yTop <- sum(y[top]); nTop <- sum(top)
>   yMid <- sum(y[mid]); nMid <- sum(mid)
> 
>   # Bayesian A/B test (Gronau, Raj K. N., & Wagenmakers, 2021) with the default priors (priorPar); psi is the log odds ratio
>   # of group 2 (top-tier) vs. group 1 (mid-tier), so an odds ratio above 1 means the practice is more common in
>   # the top-tier journals
>   set.seed(seed)
>   fit  <- abtest::ab_test(data = list(y1 = yMid, n1 = nMid, y2 = yTop, n2 = nTop),
>                           prior_par = priorPar, posterior = TRUE, nsamples = nSamples)
>   post <- fit$post$H1   # posterior samples under the alternative hypothesis (psi can differ from 0)
>   orQ   <- quantile(post$or, c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))                     # posterior median and 95% interval of the odds ratio
>   diffQ <- quantile(100 * (post$p2 - post$p1), c(0.5, 0.025, 0.975))   # ... of the difference in percentage points
> 
>   results[[i]] <- cbind(tests[i, ], yTop = yTop, nTop = nTop, yMid = yMid, nMid = nMid,
>                         data.frame(pctTop = 100 * yTop / nTop, pctMid = 100 * yMid / nMid,
>                                    lnBF10 = fit$logbf$bf10,   # natural log of BF10 (alternative vs. null), as in JASP's "Log(BF10)"
>                                    OR = orQ[[1]], ORlo = orQ[[2]], ORhi = orQ[[3]],
>                                    diffPP = diffQ[[1]], diffLo = diffQ[[2]], diffHi = diffQ[[3]]))
> }
> results <- do.call(rbind, results)
> resultsMain      <- filter(results, outcome %in% names(mainOutcomes))
> resultsSecondary <- filter(results, !outcome %in% names(mainOutcomes))
> reported <- rbind(filter(resultsMain, year == 2024), resultsSecondary)
> jaspCounts <- reported |>
>   transmute(comparison = paste(outcome, ifelse(is.na(year), "2004-2024", year), sep = ", "),
>             successesGroup1 = yMid, sampleSizeGroup1 = nMid,
>             successesGroup2 = yTop, sampleSizeGroup2 = nTop)

Python code

This module also assesses whether the paper’s Python code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 8 Python code files.

Execution

The Python code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 8 scripts: 3 ran without error, 5 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a requirements.txt). 1 script stopped on a file another script writes, so it was run once more after the other scripts: countExcludedArticles.py (excluded_types_by_journal.csv). Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). A script looked for 5 files in another folder than the deposit has them, so before running it once more we copied them there: Data_collection/Top_tier_journals/scrapeResults/Journals/APA_JEPG/xge_articles_cleaned.csv to Data_processing/Filtering/scrapeResults/Journals/APA/xge_articles_cleaned.csv for countMergedExclusions.py; Data_collection/Top_tier_journals/scrapeResults/Journals/Sage_PS/pss_articles_cleaned.csv to Data_processing/Filtering/scrapeResults/Journals/Sage/pss_articles_cleaned.csv for countMergedExclusions.py; Data_collection/Top_tier_journals/scrapeResults/Journals/Springer_PBR/pbr_articles_cleaned.csv to Data_processing/Filtering/scrapeResults/Journals/Springer/pbr_articles_cleaned.csv for countMergedExclusions.py; Data_collection/Top_tier_journals/scrapeResults/Journals/Wiley_DS/ds_articles_cleaned.csv to Data_processing/Filtering/scrapeResults/Journals/Wiley/ds_articles_cleaned.csv for countMergedExclusions.py; Data_collection/Top_tier_journals/scrapeResults/Journals/Elsevier_BRT_JESP/brt_articles_cleaned.csv to Data_processing/Filtering/scrapeResults/Journals/Elsevier/brt_articles_cleaned.csv for countMergedExclusions.py. Building paths from the top of the project (as with here::here()), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this.

os.chdir() in the code

1 script calls os.chdir(). This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with pass. Any such script that then ran is reproducible only after ignoring an os.chdir() that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed.

More detail

Power Analysis Check

No power analyses were detected.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.
